questions.prompt: Explain the Propeller Torque Effect (PTE) -- its causes, effects, and how to minimise it. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Explain what you understand about the Propeller Torque Effect, including its causes and effects and how it affects PPG flight. What aspects influence the extent of the effect, and steps to be taken to minimise the consequences.

options.label: A
options.text: Caused by thinner air at higher density altitude reducing propeller bite and available thrust, most noticeable on hot days or at higher elevations -- countered by richening the carburettor mixture, reducing pitch slightly, and allowing a longer take-off run to compensate for the reduced power available.

options.label: B
options.text: An equal-and-opposite reaction to the spinning propeller rolls the motor/pilot over to one side (e.g. right, on an anti-clockwise prop), lowering that shoulder and inducing a bank/turn that way -- worse at higher power; reduced passively (uneven carabiner heights or extra weight on the low side) or actively (differential speedbar, weight shift, asymmetric trim, counter-steer).

options.label: C
options.text: Caused by gyroscopic precession acting on the spinning propeller disc, so any force applied is felt roughly 90 degrees further around the rotation rather than where it was applied -- most noticeable during pitch changes such as sharp braking or sudden power increases, and corrected by gradually easing off power, letting the wing settle level, then reapplying power smoothly.

options.label: D
options.text: Caused by an out-of-balance crankshaft or propeller, showing up as frame and cage vibration that worsens as RPM rises through certain bands -- reduced by having the propeller professionally balanced, retorquing the motor mounts, and checking the drive belt or gearbox for wear at regular service intervals.

questions.prompt: Describe the Gyroscopic Aspects of a spinning propeller, particularly Gyroscopic Precession, and its dangers in PPG flight. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Describe the Gyroscopic Aspects, with particular emphasis on Gyroscopic Precession. What it is, what causes it and how it affects PPG flight and the resulting dangers thereof. Detail some examples, including resulting action and powered paraglider behaviour.

options.label: A
options.text: A resonance effect where the propeller, cage and frame vibrate together in sync at certain RPM ranges, most noticeable as a buzzing felt through the harness and risers -- corrected by briefly avoiding that RPM band during cruise and having the propeller checked for balance at the next service.

options.label: B
options.text: A force applied to the spinning prop disc is felt not where it's applied, but 90 degrees further around the rotation -- most noticeable when pitch changes (e.g. sharp braking or sudden full power causes the pilot to lean back), yawing the motor sharply to one side with thrust pushed off-line; recovery is to gradually back off power, wait for level flight, then slowly reapply power.

options.label: C
options.text: A reduction in propeller efficiency at higher altitude caused by thinner air reducing blade bite, most noticeable on hot days or at elevated take-off sites -- corrected by adjusting the carburettor mixture richer and allowing extra distance for the take-off run to compensate.

options.label: D
options.text: An equal-and-opposite reaction torque that rolls the motor and pilot to one side under power, worse at higher RPM and higher power settings -- corrected with differential speedbar, asymmetric trim tab settings, or a deliberate weight shift toward the high side to counter the roll tendency.

questions.prompt: Describe the three causes of Asymmetric Blade Thrust (ABT) and its effect. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Describe the three causes of Asymmetric Blade Thrust and its effect. What factors influence the extent of the problem and how can it be reduced.

options.label: A
options.text: Caused by crosswind gusts during the take-off run, thermic conditions kicking up turbulence shortly after launch, and the pilot's own weight shift while adjusting the harness in flight -- producing brief, momentary roll input that is easily corrected with normal brake and weight-shift technique; not a persistent handling problem once airborne.

options.label: B
options.text: Caused by asymmetric riser length from uneven stretch over time, an off-centre reserve parachute shifting the harness balance, and uneven brake line trim from repeated hard landings -- producing a constant, gentle turn to one side rather than an oscillation; fixed by re-trimming the risers and brake lines to manufacturer specification and rechecking with a proper hang-check.

options.label: C
options.text: Caused by an unbalanced propeller creating uneven centrifugal loading, uneven fuel distribution reaching each cylinder on multi-cylinder engines, and a worn carburettor diaphragm losing its seal -- producing a steady vibration felt through the frame and cage that worsens with RPM; fixed by replacing the propeller, the diaphragm, and rebalancing the drive train at the next service interval.

options.label: D
options.text: Three causes combine to push more thrust onto the left side of the prop disc (higher blade airspeed descending on the left, increased angle of attack on the left as the motor tilts back, and less pilot-body shielding on the left as the motor yaws right) -- producing continuous, uncommanded left-right oscillations that worsen with brake input; fixed by keeping the prop disc close to vertical via a proper hang-check, adjusted attachment points/harness trim, or reduced power.

questions.prompt: Explain why PPGs usually have higher attachment points than free-flight harnesses, and the trade-offs of high vs low attachments. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Explain why powered paragliders usually have higher Attachment Points (riser attachments) than free-flight harnesses. Describe the various methods of attachments and the advantages and disadvantages of each.

options.label: A
options.text: Higher attachments give noticeably better weight-shift and turn response than a fixed low attachment; lower attachments give better roll stability but require much longer brake lines that risk fouling the propeller cage on a hard flare, and released toggles are correspondingly harder to regrab quickly.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower attachments are used exclusively on powered units for safety reasons and to keep the centre of gravity low, while higher attachments are reserved for free-flight harnesses where weight-shift is the primary control input rather than a powered climb.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher attachments give better stability than free-flight harnesses (with the trade-off that released toggles can be harder to regrab, and brake lines must be longer and closer to the prop); lower attachments give better weight-shift and are more stable than a movable side bar, with shorter, more comfortable brake lines.

options.label: D
options.text: Attachment height makes little practical difference to stability or weight-shift response once the harness is properly hang-checked -- it comes down mostly to pilot comfort, harness style, and whichever position the manufacturer set the risers at during construction.

questions.prompt: Discuss running-in of a new engine -- purpose, procedure and precautions. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Discuss running-in of new engines, the purpose thereof, procedures and precautions. Cover aspects of carb tuning, ratio of oil mixtures, vibration problems, loosening fittings, etc.

options.label: A
options.text: Running-in is mainly about getting the carburettor tuning correct for the site's altitude and temperature -- the piston, crankshaft and bearings settle in naturally during the first few normal flights, so no special idle-and-cool cycling routine, vibration check, or fitting inspection is really necessary beforehand at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the engine at full power for around 10 minutes on first start-up so the piston rings seat against the cylinder wall quickly under load, then let it idle for cool-down for the remainder of that first session before checking the carb tuning and oil mixture are correct for the site's altitude, and looking over the whole unit for any vibration or fittings that worked loose along the way.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave the engine idling continuously for a full hour without ever raising the RPM above idle, letting the piston and rings bed in slowly at low load, then fly the unit normally from the very next start-up once the hour of idling is complete, the engine has fully cooled, and a quick check for loose fittings and correct carb tuning has been done.

options.label: D
options.text: Following the manufacturer's specification: idle 5 minutes, switch off and cool 5 minutes, idle again, briefly take it to around 2000rpm then back to idle, cool again -- repeating while raising the ceiling by about 1000rpm each cycle up to full rpm (held no longer than 30 seconds) -- to let the piston, crankshaft and bearings settle in gradually, checking for vibration, loose fittings, correct carb tuning for altitude, and the right oil mixture throughout.

questions.prompt: Comment on fuel mixtures, oil types, and running-in considerations. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Comment on Fuel Mixtures with specific reference to oil types (i.e. Synthetic vs Mineral oils), mixture ratio's and running-in considerations.

options.label: A
options.text: Mineral oil is generally preferred over synthetic for two-stroke paramotor engines because of its higher flash point and resistance to breakdown under heat, and the fuel mixture should be progressively leaned out as the engine works through its running-in period.

options.label: B
options.text: Oil type makes little real difference to engine protection provided the mixture ratio itself is correct for the manufacturer's specification; running-in actually calls for a slightly leaner mixture than normal cruise to help the rings seat faster.

options.label: C
options.text: Always follow the manufacturer's specified oil and mixture ratio; use synthetic oil, which has a much higher flash point (temperature breakdown) than mineral oil; a richer mixture is needed during running-in, tapering off once the engine is broken in.

options.label: D
options.text: Synthetic and mineral oils have essentially the same flash point and heat-breakdown resistance; the mixture ratio only needs to be richened once the engine is fully broken in and being flown at higher power settings regularly.

questions.prompt: Discuss heat-seizure of engines -- causes, extent of damage, repairs, and prevention. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Discuss heat-seizure of engines, causes thereof, assessing extent of damage, resulting repairs required, and preventative action.

options.label: A
options.text: Caused by low compression from gradually worn piston rings over many hours of normal running -- unlike a sudden seizure this develops slowly over time, and once compression drops far enough it always requires a full engine replacement rather than a lesser repair, rebuild, or simple honing of the cylinder wall.

options.label: B
options.text: Caused specifically by using synthetic oil instead of mineral oil in the fuel mixture, which some engines are said not to tolerate well at sustained high RPM on a hot day -- prevented simply by switching back to a mineral-oil mixture, keeping the same ratio the manufacturer specifies, and avoiding a lean carburettor setting.

options.label: C
options.text: Caused by excess heat or inadequate lubrication -- a carburettor set too lean, wrong spark plug, old fuel, or a leaking gasket -- melting and smearing the piston onto the cylinder wall; ranges from burnt rings to a fully damaged piston/sleeve; repaired by replacing damaged parts, honing if needed, then running-in again; prevented with the correct fuel/oil mixture, a carb set slightly rich rather than lean, and tight nuts/bolts to stop gasket leaks.

options.label: D
options.text: Caused by over-lubrication combined with an over-rich mixture fouling the spark plug and washing oil off the cylinder wall -- fixed by leaning the carburettor slightly, correcting the oil ratio, and replacing the fouled plug, with no further internal repair usually needed beyond that, though nuts and bolts should still be checked for tightness and any leaking gasket replaced afterwards.

questions.prompt: Briefly describe the Semi-Circular Separation Rule. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Briefly describe the concept of the Semi-Circular Separation Rule, as pertaining to air-traffic separation. (no need to reproduce the actual table here)

options.label: A
options.text: Provides horizontal separation below 1500ft AGL in uncontrolled airspace by requiring aircraft on opposite headings to stay at least one nautical mile apart laterally, regardless of the flight level or altitude either aircraft happens to be flying at.

options.label: B
options.text: Requires every aircraft flying above 1500ft AGL to use even flight levels only, regardless of magnetic track flown, with the 500ft VFR offset applied only inside controlled airspace rather than in the open uncontrolled airspace most PPG pilots use.

options.label: C
options.text: Applies only within controlled airspace and splits traffic by altitude band rather than by magnetic track, with air traffic control assigning each aircraft an altitude band on first contact rather than pilots self-selecting a flight level.

options.label: D
options.text: Provides vertical separation above 1500ft AGL in uncontrolled airspace by splitting tracks into two regions (000-179 degrees and 180-359 degrees): the first flies odd flight levels, the second even, with 500ft added for VFR (e.g. 5500ft vs 6500ft).

questions.prompt: Explain the Following Line Rule. Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Explain the principles and application of the Following Line Rule.

options.label: A
options.text: At or below 1500ft AGL, when following a line feature (road, railway, power line, canal, coastline, etc.) within one nautical mile, fly to the right of it unless ATC instructs otherwise.

options.label: B
options.text: Line features such as roads, railways and power lines must always be crossed at right angles rather than followed alongside in either direction, to keep pilots from being mistaken for traffic tracking the feature itself.

options.label: C
options.text: At or below 1500ft AGL, always fly to the left of any line feature you are following -- road, railway, power line, canal or coastline -- regardless of any instruction given by air traffic control on frequency at the time.

options.label: D
options.text: The rule only applies above 1500ft AGL, and requires aircraft following a line feature within one nautical mile to keep it on their right-hand side at all times, with no exception even when instructed otherwise by ATC.

questions.prompt: What do VMC, VFR, QNE, AGL, FL, UTC, CTR and FAR stand for? Which of the following correctly defines all eight?
questions.print_prompt: What do the following abbreviations stand for, and give a brief description of each: VMC, VFR, QNE, AGL, FL, UTC, CTR, FAR.

options.label: A
options.text: VMC = Visual Meteorological Conditions (clear of cloud, minimum visibility); VFR = Visual Flight Rules (visual reference, weather, separation and clearance rules); QNE = altimeter subscale set to standard pressure 1013.2 hPa; AGL = Above Ground Level; FL = Flight Level, altitude on the QNE setting expressed without the last two zeros; UTC = Universal Co-ordinated Time (no timezone/DST); CTR = Control Zone around an airfield, roughly 10x30nm, ground level up to about 6500ft; FAR = (South African) Restricted Area, entry restricted, usually needing military/authority permission.

options.label: B
options.text: VMC = Visual Meteorological Conditions with no defined minimum visibility requirement anywhere; VFR = rules that apply only to night flying under visual reference; QNE = altimeter set to 1013.2 hPa but only used above Flight Level 200; AGL = height measured above the highest obstacle within the area rather than the ground; FL = altitude expressed in metres rather than feet on the QNE setting; UTC = a time zone used only by air traffic control staff, never by pilots; CTR = airspace with no defined vertical limit at all; FAR = an area civilians may enter freely at any time without restriction.

options.label: C
options.text: VMC = Visual Flight Rules governing when radio calls are mandatory; VFR = Visual Meteorological Conditions describing cloud cover only; QNE = altimeter subscale set to the departure aerodrome's local pressure; AGL = altitude measured above mean sea level rather than the ground; FL = Flight Level shown with the last two zeros still included; UTC = local time adjusted for daylight saving where it applies; CTR = a Restricted Area drawn around a military base; FAR = a Control Zone drawn around a civilian airfield.

options.label: D
options.text: VMC = clear of cloud with an 8km minimum flight visibility and no other requirement; VFR = a set of rules that apply only above Flight Level 100 in controlled airspace; QNE = altimeter set to the nearest airfield's current QNH reading; AGL = height measured from mean sea level rather than the ground below; FL = altitude flown on the QNH setting rather than standard pressure; UTC = the time kept in the pilot's own home timezone; CTR = an area civilian aircraft are always prohibited from entering; FAR = a race-track shaped danger area drawn around a city centre.

questions.prompt: How often should you make general radio announcements in flight? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: How often do you need to make general radio announcements while in flight?

options.label: A
options.text: There's no fixed interval (it isn't simply every 5 minutes) -- announce whenever you change direction or altitude, and more frequently in areas with more air traffic.

options.label: B
options.text: Only when specifically instructed to make a call by air traffic control on frequency -- self-initiated position reports are discouraged in uncontrolled airspace since they add unnecessary radio chatter.

options.label: C
options.text: Only once, immediately after you first depart from the take-off field -- no further position or intention announcements are required for the remainder of the flight, even if your routing or altitude changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Every 5 minutes exactly by the clock, regardless of whether you have changed direction or altitude in that time, and regardless of how much other air traffic is operating in the same area at that moment.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a general radio broadcast for your area. Which of the following correctly follows the standard structure?
questions.print_prompt: Write an example of a general radio broadcast announcement for your area.

options.label: A
options.text: Structured around just a call sign and current position -- e.g. 'Traffic, Delta Delta Delta, overhead Bethlehem' -- with altitude, routing and intentions treated as optional extras only included when the pilot personally judges them necessary for that particular call.

options.label: B
options.text: Structured as CAPARI -- Call sign, Aircraft type, Position, Altitude, Routing, Intentions -- e.g. 'Traffic on 124.8, Delta Delta Delta, is a Motorised Paraglider 5 miles south of Bethlehem, below 500ft, heading north toward Bethlehem airport on a pleasure flight, Delta Delta Delta'.

options.label: C
options.text: Structured as Aircraft type, Fuel state, Souls on board, and Estimated Time of Arrival -- the standard format used for any general aviation position report, regardless of whether the flight itself is powered or unpowered.

options.label: D
options.text: Structured as Call sign, Altitude and Squawk code only -- e.g. 'Delta Delta Delta, 500ft, squawking 7000' -- since position and intentions are assumed to already be covered automatically by radar in that area.

questions.prompt: When should you inspect your motor for potential problems (nuts, bolts, rubbers, belt, etc)? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: When should you inspect your motor for potential problems (nuts, bolts, rubbers, belt, etc)?

options.label: A
options.text: Before and after every flight (pre-flight and post-flight checks are equally important), plus at the manufacturer's specified hourly intervals for parts like piston/rings, spark plugs, and carb diaphragms.

options.label: B
options.text: Only after any flight where something felt unusual in the air, such as extra vibration or a rough-running engine -- routine, uneventful flights don't generally call for a hands-on inspection afterwards.

options.label: C
options.text: At the manufacturer's specified hourly service intervals only -- a quick visual check before each individual flight isn't strictly necessary provided the unit was serviced correctly and on schedule.

options.label: D
options.text: Before each flight only -- a thorough pre-flight walk-round is essential, but post-flight checks become optional once a pilot has built up enough hours to reliably feel when something on the unit isn't right.

questions.prompt: If your engine kill-switch fails while about to land, what should you do? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: If you are about to land and discover that your engine kill-switch is not functional, what would you do and how would you kill the engine?

options.label: A
options.text: Disconnect the harness carabiners from the motor while still in flight and continue the landing approach on the wing alone, leaving the running motor to free-fall separately once clear of the pilot.

options.label: B
options.text: Climb to at least 500ft AGL first, then try flooding the carburettor, covering the air filter/carb intake, pinching the fuel line, pulling the spark plug lead (not the plug itself), closing the fuel or air valve, or using the secondary safety switch if fitted.

options.label: C
options.text: Land immediately regardless of your current altitude, treating the approach and landing as the priority, and only switch the ignition off at the magneto or battery terminal once the unit is safely down on the ground.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the throttle to maximum power deliberately, aiming to force the engine to flood itself on excess fuel and stall out on its own, then glide the remainder of the approach with the propeller stopped.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to have your speed-bar fitted? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: Why is it important to have your speed-bar fitted?

options.label: A
options.text: To increase airspeed in strong or unexpected wind -- check your wing's manual first, as on some wings using speedbar and brake together when trimmed out can cause a serious collapse.

options.label: B
options.text: To reduce airspeed and give a more controlled, slower approach on landing, particularly useful in gusty conditions where extra margin above stall speed is wanted during the final stages of the flare.

options.label: C
options.text: To trim the wing for comfortable, hands-free straight and level cruising over longer distances, freeing the pilot's hands for navigation, radio calls, or adjusting the harness during extended flights.

options.label: D
options.text: To increase glide ratio when searching for lift in weak thermal conditions, letting the pilot cover more ground per foot of height lost while working a thermal that hasn't yet built up much strength.

questions.prompt: What are the benefits and usages of trim-tabs on a powered wing? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: What are the benefits and usages of having trim tabs on a powered wing?

options.label: A
options.text: Set, they give a higher angle of attack that helps on take-off; released, they give higher speed and faster inflation; different left/right settings can also help counter torque effect.

options.label: B
options.text: They only affect trim speed during normal cruise flight -- take-off performance and canopy inflation behaviour are essentially unaffected by whatever position the trim tabs are set to before launch.

options.label: C
options.text: Set, they reduce the wing's angle of attack to shorten the take-off run; released, they slow the wing down noticeably, which is useful for a softer, more controlled landing in confined spaces.

options.label: D
options.text: They exist mainly for pilot comfort during long flights and have no meaningful aerodynamic effect on either the take-off run or how the canopy inflates during the launch sequence.

questions.prompt: If you are flying with a friend, what must you beware of? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: If you are flying with a friend, what must you beware of?

options.label: A
options.text: Only wind direction needs watching when flying near others -- spacing between gliders and right-of-way in a turn are set entirely by air traffic control rather than by the pilots themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Only radio communication matters for safe formation flying -- a good visual lookout for other gliders isn't really necessary provided everyone announces their position regularly on frequency.

options.label: C
options.text: Stay aware of nearby gliders, look before you turn, keep enough separation to avoid touching wingtips, watch for prop wash, and observe right-of-way rules.

options.label: D
options.text: Only your own altitude and heading really matter -- other pilots flying nearby are responsible for keeping clear of you and adjusting their own flight path to avoid any conflict.

questions.prompt: If you accidentally bump wingtips with a buddy in flight, what's the correct course of action for both pilots? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: If you are flying alongside a buddy and you accidentally bump wingtips, what is the correct course of action for both pilots?

options.label: A
options.text: The left-hand pilot climbs while the right-hand pilot descends, with both maintaining their existing heading rather than turning, so as to gain vertical separation without changing course.

options.label: B
options.text: The left-hand pilot decreases power and turns left; the right-hand pilot increases power and turns right -- both establish vertical and horizontal separation by turning away from each other.

options.label: C
options.text: Both pilots should turn toward each other and try to match altitude, re-establishing eye contact so each can visually confirm the other's wing hasn't been damaged before continuing the flight.

options.label: D
options.text: Both pilots should cut power immediately and glide straight ahead on the existing heading until well clear of one another, without turning left or right in either direction.

questions.prompt: What is a safe distance/height when flying near the coast, a lake or a dam? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: If you are flying near the coast (or lake or dam), what is a safe distance and height to go out over the water?

options.label: A
options.text: Stay within a 1:1 distance-to-height ratio at all times, and wear a personal life jacket rather than an auto-floatation device fitted to the unit itself when planning to fly out over open water.

options.label: B
options.text: There's no fixed ratio to worry about -- any distance out over the water is acceptable provided you remain above roughly 1000ft AGL for the entire time you're out over the lake, dam or coastline.

options.label: C
options.text: Never exceed a 2:1 distance-to-height ratio, always stay within gliding range of the shore, and carry an auto-floatation device (e.g. power float/Agama) if flying over water.

options.label: D
options.text: A 4:1 distance-to-height ratio is considered safe provided the water is calm and you remain reasonably close to shore, without needing any additional floatation equipment fitted or carried.

questions.prompt: Why would you log your flying hours?

options.label: A
options.text: Mainly to keep servicing records for the engine -- training progress and licence applications are tracked separately by the CFI using the syllabus sign-off sheet, not the pilot's own personal log.

options.label: B
options.text: Mainly to record training progress toward a rating -- proof of experience for licence applications comes from the CFI's own records, and engine hours are tracked on a separate service log kept with the unit.

options.label: C
options.text: It matters only if you plan to compete or apply for an instructor rating later on -- for an ordinary recreational pilot flying for pleasure, keeping a personal log of hours isn't really necessary.

options.label: D
options.text: To record training progress, support licence and renewal applications, provide proof of experience and licences received, and track engine hours for servicing intervals.

questions.prompt: If you double your flying height above the ground, by what factor is the landing area reachable by gliding increased (in the event of an engine-out)?

options.label: A
options.text: Doubled only -- engine-out glide distance simply doubles foot-for-foot as height above the ground increases, with no compounding effect on the area reachable.

options.label: B
options.text: Increased by only 50% -- glide ratio flattens out noticeably as altitude increases, so doubling height adds far less reachable area than it would at low level.

options.label: C
options.text: Tripled -- every extra 100ft of height adds three times the horizontal glide range achievable before the wing reaches the ground in an engine-out scenario.

options.label: D
options.text: Four times greater -- doubling your height above the ground quadruples the ground area reachable within gliding range, since that reachable area is a circle whose size grows with the square of the glide radius.

questions.prompt: How far do you need to remain away from cloud, vertically and horizontally? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: How far do you need to remain away from clouds? Vertically and horizontally.

options.label: A
options.text: You must remain at least 1000ft vertically and 1500ft horizontally from cloud at all altitudes, with no lower-level exemption.

options.label: B
options.text: Below 1000ft AGL you need 500ft vertical and 1000ft horizontal clearance; above 1000ft up to FL100 you must remain clear of cloud entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: Cloud clearance rules apply above FL100 in controlled airspace -- below that level you may fly through cloud freely provided you remain in radio contact with the nearest air traffic control unit.

options.label: D
options.text: Below 1000ft AGL you must remain clear of cloud (no set distance specified); from 1000ft AGL up to FL100 you need at least 2000ft vertically and 500ft horizontally from cloud.

questions.prompt: When flying around sunset, what is the latest you may remain in the air?
questions.print_prompt: When flying around sunset, what is the latest you may remain in the air?

options.label: A
options.text: Official sunset itself only -- no further flying is permitted after that exact time is reached.

options.label: B
options.text: 30 minutes after official sunset, local time as published in the AIP.

options.label: C
options.text: Until last light, entirely at the pilot's own discretion on the day.

options.label: D
options.text: 15 minutes after official sunset, local time as published in the AIP.

questions.prompt: What do you need (licensing and equipment) before you may take a passenger for a tandem flight? Which of the following correctly covers this?
questions.print_prompt: What do you need before you may take a passenger for a tandem flight on your paramotor? (in terms of licensing and equipment)

options.label: A
options.text: A valid Paramotor tandem licence, a motor with enough power for the extra weight, a harness that fits the passenger, a wing rated to carry the combined weight, and signed indemnity forms.

options.label: B
options.text: A tandem-rated wing is the only extra requirement -- the pilot's normal licence, motor and harness otherwise cover carrying a passenger without any further paperwork or fitting checks.

options.label: C
options.text: Any current PPG licence together with verbal consent from the passenger and a helmet for each person -- no separate tandem rating or additional equipment checks are required beyond that.

options.label: D
options.text: SAHPA membership in good standing plus the passenger's own signed medical declaration -- no additional licence, harness fit, or wing-rating checks apply beyond those two documents.

questions.prompt: A lighter all-up take-off weight will increase:

options.label: A
options.text: Take-off distance.

options.label: B
options.text: Climb rate.

options.label: C
options.text: Power-off stall speed.

options.label: D
options.text: Power-on stall speed.

questions.prompt: A heavier all-up take-off weight will increase:

options.label: A
options.text: Stall speed alone -- airspeed and take-off run stay roughly the same regardless of how much total weight the pilot happens to be carrying on that particular flight.

options.label: B
options.text: Overall flying airspeed, stall speed, and take-off run all increase together, along with a higher internal cell pressure needed to keep the wing's shape stable at the higher wing loading.

options.label: C
options.text: Take-off run alone -- stall speed and airspeed are set mainly by the wing's own design rather than by the pilot's total take-off weight on any given day.

options.label: D
options.text: Overall airspeed alone -- stall speed actually decreases slightly as the total take-off weight increases, contrary to what most pilots would expect to happen.

questions.prompt: The _______ is an imaginary straight line drawn through an airfoil (wing) from the leading edge to the trailing edge.

options.label: A
options.text: Relative wind line.

options.label: B
options.text: Angle of attack.

options.label: C
options.text: Camber line.

options.label: D
options.text: Chord line.

questions.prompt: Angle of attack is defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: The angle between the horizon and the chord line.

options.label: B
options.text: The angle between the wing chord line and the vertical tail.

options.label: C
options.text: The angle between the wing chord line and the relative airflow.

options.label: D
options.text: The angle between the horizon and the relative wind.

questions.prompt: A stall occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: The critical angle of attack is exceeded.

options.label: B
options.text: The engine loses power unexpectedly.

options.label: C
options.text: The nose rises too far above the horizon.

options.label: D
options.text: The airspeed drops below trim speed.

questions.prompt: Trimspeed is defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: Flying as slowly as possible with trim tabs fully retracted.

options.label: B
options.text: Flying at roughly 50% throttle with light brake pressure held.

options.label: C
options.text: Flying hands-up, off speedbar, with trim tabs set to neutral.

options.label: D
options.text: Flying hands-up, on full speedbar, with trim tabs set to neutral.

questions.prompt: In heavy turbulence it is safest to minimise deflations by flying:

options.label: A
options.text: As fast as possible, held well past trim speed.

options.label: B
options.text: At trim speed, hands up and off the speedbar.

options.label: C
options.text: Downwind of any high ground you can find nearby.

options.label: D
options.text: As slowly as possible, flown close to stall.

questions.prompt: You are on a head-on collision course with another aircraft in open areas. You should avoid the other aircraft by:

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Climbing steeply to pass above the other aircraft's current flight path instead.

options.label: C
options.text: Descending quickly to pass below the other aircraft's current flight path instead.

options.label: D
options.text: Turning to the right, per the standard head-on right-of-way rule.

questions.prompt: You are flying north in straight and level flight with a True Airspeed of 38km/h. The wind at your altitude is from 180 degrees at 10km/h. What is your groundspeed?

options.label: B
options.text: 38 km/h

options.label: C
options.text: 48 km/h

options.label: D
options.text: 10 km/h

questions.prompt: A magnetic compass is accurate:

options.label: A
options.text: Only in straight and level flight at a constant speed.

options.label: B
options.text: In any attitude, including turns, climbs and descents.

options.label: C

questions.prompt: You would most likely find turbulent flying in conditions near:

options.label: A
options.text: Near high, wispy cirrus clouds well above the altitudes normal PPG flying takes place at.

options.label: B
options.text: Near cumulus clouds, especially tall, building cumulus with strong vertical development.

options.label: C
options.text: Near fog or low-lying mist sitting close to the ground on a calm, still morning.

options.label: D
options.text: Near flat, featureless stratus cloud layers that show little or no vertical development at all.

questions.prompt: You would likely find turbulence:

options.label: A
options.text: Near mountains, during the mid-afternoon heating peak, deep inland, and downwind of buildings -- all of these increase turbulence.

options.label: B
options.text: Mostly near mountains -- the time of day and terrain elsewhere generally make only a small difference to how rough the air feels.

options.label: C
options.text: Mainly directly over open water, well away from any terrain features, buildings or other obstacles that might disturb the airflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Mainly in the early morning hours, before the ground has had a chance to warm up and start generating any convective activity.

questions.prompt: Why does SAHPA exist?

options.label: A
options.text: Mainly to manufacture and formally approve equipment sold to pilots in South Africa, similar to a national standards body.

options.label: B
options.text: Mainly to act as a social club connecting pilots around the country, without taking on much of a regulatory or insurance role.

options.label: C
options.text: Mainly to organise national competitions, record badge flights, and rank pilots on a national scoreboard for each discipline.

options.label: D
options.text: To keep the sport self-regulating, provide third-party aviation insurance, run a safety-oriented licensing system, and give the sport international recognition.

questions.prompt: What is the very last safety action to perform prior to starting an engine?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm there is a sufficient quantity of fuel on board for the planned flight.

options.label: B
options.text: Call "clear prop" and confirm the prop area is clear of people.

options.label: C
options.text: Complete one final full walk-around pre-flight inspection of the whole unit.

options.label: D
options.text: Double-check the fuel-to-oil mixture ratio is correctly blended for that tank.

questions.prompt: Considering density altitude, your motor and wing would perform better on:

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Cold humid days.

options.label: C

questions.prompt: When may you enter a Restricted Area (FAR)?

options.label: A
options.text: After receiving permission from the appropriate authority.

options.label: B
options.text: Only at weekends, when the areas are officially closed.

options.label: C
options.text: Never -- Restricted Areas may not be entered under any circumstance.

options.label: D
options.text: Whenever you wish, provided you exercise extreme caution.

questions.prompt: When may you enter a Prohibited Area (FAP)?

options.label: A
options.text: Any time between official sunset and official sunrise, when the area is considered officially inactive.

options.label: B
options.text: With informal verbal permission from whichever agency happens to be controlling that airspace at the time.

options.label: C
options.text: Never at all -- Prohibited Areas may not be entered under any circumstance, no matter the reason given.

options.label: D
options.text: Only with a written waiver from the CAA Administrator or their designee.

questions.prompt: What frequency is used for emergency communications?
Take-off run distance is increased by:

options.label: A
options.text: A lighter headwind, higher altitude, higher humidity, and lower QNH -- all of these increase the take-off run.

options.label: B
options.text: Mainly a stronger headwind -- the other factors listed make comparatively little practical difference to the length of run needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Mainly higher altitude -- humidity and the current QNH setting are largely negligible by comparison for take-off performance.

options.label: D
options.text: Mainly a lower QNH reading -- wind strength and altitude have comparatively little effect on the length of the take-off run.

questions.prompt: Carb mixture adjustment should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Adjusted the same way regardless of altitude, QNH or humidity, since none of those affect mixture in practice.

options.label: B
options.text: Richened as altitude decreases (the denser, lower air needs more fuel for the same ratio).

options.label: C
options.text: Richened whenever the QNH reading is low that day, regardless of the actual altitude being flown at the time.

options.label: D
options.text: Richened for higher humidity conditions, since the theory goes that damp air needs extra fuel to combust cleanly.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true, regarding altimeter settings and radio calls?

options.label: A
options.text: Below 1500ft AGL the altimeter subscale is set to local QNH and altitude is given in feet; above transition altitude it's set to QNE, and altitude is then given as a Flight Level.

options.label: B
options.text: Altitude is always given in feet throughout the flight, even once the subscale has been switched over to the standard QNE setting above the transition altitude.

options.label: C
options.text: The altimeter subscale is always kept set to standard pressure QNE regardless of altitude flown, with altitude reported in feet at every stage of the flight, never as a Flight Level.

options.label: D
options.text: Below 1500ft AGL the subscale is set to QNE while above transition altitude it's set to local QNH, with altitude given as a Flight Level only below that transition layer.

questions.prompt: Which one is true regarding rate of climb?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased when flying into a headwind and correspondingly reduced when flying with a tailwind.

options.label: B
options.text: Affected by your throttle setting; unaffected by windspeed or direction.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced when flying into a headwind and correspondingly increased when flying with a tailwind.

options.label: D
options.text: Unaffected by throttle setting at all -- determined entirely by the wind's speed and direction.

questions.prompt: Angle of climb is:

options.label: A
options.text: Mainly increased in a headwind -- power setting and trim speed make comparatively little difference to the resulting angle of climb.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced in a headwind and increased at a faster airspeed trim, the reverse of how rate of climb typically behaves in those same conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: Increased in a headwind, increased with added power, reduced at a faster airspeed trim, and reduced in turns.

options.label: D
options.text: Mainly increased with added power -- wind strength and trim speed setting make comparatively little difference to the resulting angle of climb.

questions.prompt: When taking off in thermic conditions, you are 10 metres up when you fly into a thermal and the glider pitches back. Your reaction is:

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain roughly 3/4 power and catch the pendulum as the glider surges forward.

options.label: B
options.text: Come to idle power immediately and pump the brakes rapidly to try to force the glider back overhead.

options.label: C
options.text: Go to full power immediately while also increasing brake pressure to try to punch straight through the thermal.

options.label: D
options.text: Do nothing at all and simply let the glider find its own way to recover without any pilot input.
